props.title: The Hot Rock
props.initialSlug: Bungling crooks attempt to steal diamond four times

sections.content: **The Hot Rock** (1972) brilliantly subverts heist movie expectations by focusing on a gang that keeps having to steal the same diamond multiple times. Robert Redford's Dortmunder character, adapted from Donald E. Westlake's novels, brings a weary professionalism that contrasts sharply with the glossy confidence of contemporaries like **Thomas Crown Affair** (1968). Director Peter Yates, fresh off **Bullitt** (1968), applies his gritty street-level authenticity to create a heist comedy that feels more like a series of increasingly desperate Plan Bs than a slick caper.

sections.content: The film established a distinctly American take on the heist genre, influencing later comedic capers like **Quick Change** (1990) and **Out of Sight** (1998). William Goldman's razor-sharp screenplay maintains the novel's sardonic wit while adding layers of character complexity, particularly in the relationship between Dortmunder and his brother-in-law Kelp (George Segal). Their dynamic would later inspire similar pairings in films like **Bottle Rocket** (1996).

The New York location shooting captures a grittier early 70s city than the more polished **The Taking of Pelham One Two Three** (1974) or **Dog Day Afternoon** (1975). Yates uses this authentic backdrop to ground the increasingly outlandish scenarios, from prison breaks to helicopter escapes, in a tangible reality that makes the comedy land harder. SUBHEAD: Evolution of the Comic Heist Film

sections.content: **The Hot Rock** marked a significant shift from the ultra-cool heist films of the 1960s like **Ocean's 11** (1960) and **Topkapi** (1964). Its influence can be seen in later films that embrace failure and complications as central comedic elements, from **Small Time Crooks** (2000) to **Logan Lucky** (2017). The film's structure of multiple attempted heists targeting the same object would later be refined in movies like **Hudson Hawk** (1991), though few matched Goldman's sharp wit.
